chunks: And from him, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Nasr, from al-Husayn ibn Khalid, who said:

I asked Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) about the dowry of the Sunnah, how it became five hundred [dirhams]. He said: 'Indeed, Allah the Exalted obligated upon Himself that if a believer does not glorify Him one hundred glorifications, not exalt Him one hundred exaltations, not praise Him one hundred praisings, not declare His Oneness one hundred declarations, and not send blessings upon Muhammad and his family one hundred times, then Allah will not marry him to a Hurra' (a celestial maiden). And He made that [the Hurra] her dowry. Then Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, revealed to His Prophet to establish the dowries of the believing women as five hundred dirhams. So the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) did that. And whoever of the believers proposes to his brother for his sister's hand, and offers five hundred [dirhams], but he does not marry her to him, then he has hindered him, and deserves from Allah the Mighty and Majestic that He will not marry him to a Hurra'.'
The Sheikh (may Allah have mercy on him) said: And it is not appropriate for a man to consummate the marriage with his wife until he gives her something of her dowry, whether little or much.

key_terms.تَهْلِيلَةٍ: Declaration of Oneness (saying La ilaha illallah)
key_terms.حَوْرَاءَ: A Hurra', a celestial maiden of Paradise
key_terms.مَهْرِ السُّنَّةِ: The standard or recommended dowry established by the Prophet

ai.seo_question: What is the origin and significance of the five hundred dirham dowry in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from Al-Tusi’s *Tahdhib* elucidates the theological basis for the standard dowry (mahr al-sunnah) of five hundred dirhams, attributing its establishment to divine revelation instructing the Prophet to set this amount for believers. It uniquely connects the material transaction to a spiritual reward, suggesting that fulfilling the dowry obligation ensures the believer’s marriage to a Hurra' in paradise, while failure to do so constitutes a spiritual hindrance. The narration concludes with a practical juristic ruling emphasizing that partial payment of the mahr is a prerequisite for consummation, reinforcing the financial rights of the wife in Shia fiqh.
